figure: FIGURE 15.2, panel (a) 'Caching removes prefill work' — in-plot note f(r)=(1-S+P)/S
issue: The formula printed inside panel (a) does not reproduce the curve drawn in that panel, and the caption repeats the same formula. As rendered, the note reads f(r)=(1-S+P)/S with P=40% and S=60%. Substitution gives f(1) = (1-0.60+0.40)/0.60 = 0.80/0.60 = 1.333, i.e. 133 GFLOPs at r=1, whereas the drawn green curve starts at exactly 100 (the no-cache value) at r=1 and ends near 60-64 at r=10. The drawn series is reproduced by f(r) = S + P/r = 0.60 + 0.40/r (f(1)=1.00, f(2)=0.80, f(5)=0.68, f(10)=0.64), which is the only formula family consistent with the caption's own definitions ('P = 40% - the reusable prefix share of the prompt - and S = 60% - the unique suffix'). As printed, the note is wrong at every plotted point, and the caption's gloss 'the in-plot note's f(r)=(1-S+P)/S' propagates the error into the prose. (The exact glyphs must be confirmed against the figure source: if the source string contains an '/r' term, the same defect persists, because (1-S+P/r)/S = 1.333 at r=1.)
evidence: Recomputation from the page's own stated inputs: P=0.40, S=0.60. Printed formula: f(1) = (1-0.6+0.4)/0.6 = 1.333 -> 133 GFLOPs; f(10) = (1-0.6+0.4)/0.6 = 1.333 (no r dependence at all as read). Drawn curve: f(1) = 1.00 (100 GFLOPs, coincident with the flat 'no cache' series), f(10) ~= 0.60-0.64. Candidate correct form S + P/r: f(1)=1.00, f(2)=0.80, f(3)=0.733, f(5)=0.68, f(8)=0.65, f(10)=0.64 - matching the drawn curve's steep initial drop and its flattening toward ~0.62. The caption's own definition of reuse ('mean number of requests served from each cached prefix block, so 1 = no sharing and hence no prefix reduction') also requires f(1)=1, which the printed formula violates.
acceptance_test: Extract the exact note string from the figure source; recompute f(1), f(2), f(5), f(10) with P=0.40, S=0.60; confirm the plotted series equals the printed formula at all four points. If not, replace the note with f(r) = S + P/r (or (S*r + P)/r), update the caption gloss accordingly, and re-verify that the caption's '1 = no sharing and hence no prefix reduction' statement holds at r=1.

figure: FIGURE 15.2, panel (a) y-axis label 'Prefill FLOPs / req (G)'
issue: The left panel's y-axis is labeled in absolute units ('Prefill FLOPs / req (G)', 0-100) while the caption describes the same panel as 'prefill work vs average prefix reuse, as a percent of no-cache prefill work'. The two cannot both be true. As an absolute value the axis is also implausible: 100 GFLOPs of prefill per request corresponds to roughly 7 prompt tokens on a 7B model (2*N*T = 1.4e10*T) and to 0.7 tokens on a 70B model, so no realistic model/prompt pair yields a 100 GFLOPs prefill baseline. The plotted quantity is therefore a normalized ratio, and the axis label misrepresents it as an absolute cost. A reader who trusts the axis could conclude that prefill is trivially cheap and therefore never compute-bound - the exact misconception the surrounding chapter is trying to prevent.
evidence: Caption text on the page: 'left: prefill work vs average prefix reuse, as a percent of no-cache prefill work, lower is better'. Axis text: 'Prefill FLOPs / req (G)' with the 'no cache' series flat at 100. Prefill FLOPs check: 2 * 7e9 * T = 100e9 -> T ~= 7.1 tokens; 2 * 70e9 * T = 100e9 -> T ~= 0.71 tokens. Both are far below any realistic prompt length, confirming the axis is normalized, not absolute. The '(G)' suffix is also ambiguous between 'giga' and 'GFLOP'.
acceptance_test: Relabel the axis 'Prefill work per request (% of no-cache)' (dropping '(G)'), or state the absolute baseline in the caption (e.g. 'no-cache prefill = X GFLOPs for the canonical model and prompt') and verify X against the book's canonical workload. Confirm the caption and axis then describe the same quantity.

figure: FIGURE 15.2, caption clause 'caching raises decode goodput (right: decode goodput vs batch size, ...)'

The figure title ('Prefill caching vs batching: two independent effects') and the panel titles are consistent with the prose, so the caption is the odd element out.

Body text, same page: 'batching raises decode goodput (right plot) until bandwidth saturates, while prefix caching lowers the prefill work per repeated prompt (left plot)'. Panel (b) x-axis: 'Decode batch size'. No caching variable appears on the right panel's axes.
acceptance_test: Grep the caption source for 'raises decode goodput' and confirm the grammatical subject is 'batching'. figure: FIGURE 15.2, figure title ('two independent effects') and the body paragraph immediately below the caption

The figure title says 'two independent effects' and the body text says 'They are not competing on the same axis: the decode bottleneck is unaffected by caching.' Under continuous batching, freed prefill headroom changes how many sequences can be resident, which changes the decode batch size - precisely the quantity on the right panel's x-axis. They are not competing on the same axis: the decode bottleneck is unaffected by caching.' Figure title: 'Prefill caching vs batching: two independent effects'.

figure: TCO break-even figure (referenced in prose as "the figure"; figure itself NOT on this page or p. 291 — see FIG-291-04)
issue: The break-even arithmetic that defines the figure's break-even band is typeset with the wrong operator. As rendered, the clause reads "6,232,677.2 = 155,816.93 × 0.025" and "10,387,795.33 = 155,816.93 × 0.015". Multiplication gives 3,895.42 and 2,337.25, not the printed results. The printed results are exactly the QUOTIENTS (155,816.93 ÷ 0.025 = 6,232,677.2; 155,816.93 ÷ 0.015 = 10,387,795.33), i.e. break-even requests/month = monthly cost ÷ cost per request. The same operator appears in the 22-host clause ("6,510,426.6 = 162,760.59 × 0.025") and in the 70%×95% clause ("232,197.23 × 0.0208 = … 11.2M req/mo"). If the source glyph is actually "÷" and only the 150 dpi render is ambiguous, this is a false positive — but if the source says "×", the entire break-even derivation (the 6.2–10.4M band and the 7.5M canonical point that the figure plots) is arithmetically wrong as printed.
evidence: Recomputed from the page's own inputs: 155,816.93 ÷ 0.025 = 6,232,677.2 (printed value matches to 7 s.f.); 155,816.93 ÷ 0.015 = 10,387,795.33 (matches); 155,816.93 ÷ 0.0208 = 7,491,198.56 (matches the printed canonical point); 162,760.59 ÷ 0.025 = 6,510,423.6 vs printed 6,510,426.6 (Δ = 3.0, i.e. 5e-5 relative — rounding of the unrounded monthly cost, not a finding); 162,760.59 ÷ 0.0208 = 7,825,028.4 (matches printed 7,825,028); 232,197.23 ÷ 0.0208 = 11,163,328 ≈ 11.2M (matches printed). Every printed RESULT is a quotient; no printed result is a product. Multiplication by the same factors yields values off by 1,600× and 4,444× respectively.
acceptance_test: Open the source for printed p. 270 and confirm the glyph. If it is "×", replace with "÷" in all four instances (21-host low end, 21-host high end, 22-host low end, 70%×95% case) and re-verify that each printed result still equals cost ÷ price-per-request. Then confirm the figure's break-even band endpoints (6.2M and 10.4M) and its canonical-price marker (7.5M at $0.0208) are unchanged and still consistent with the corrected equations.

figure: TCO feasible served-volume figure (the figure that "shades and labels" the infeasible region; not present on this page)
issue: The feasible served-volume bound — the quantity that determines where the figure shades the infeasible region — is stated with a broken numeric chain, and the printed value is 1,000× too small. The sentence reads: "the fixed 21-host fleet is sized for the 40 rps peak over the canonical active window of 62,000 active seconds/month (6,240,000 requests × 10 rps), so the most it can serve is 40 × 62,000 = 2,560,000 = 24,960 requests/month. Everything to the right of 24,960 on the x-axis — the plot runs to 10^8 — is infeasible …". Three separate errors: (i) the active window is 62,000 s but the same page later calls it "the canonical 624,000-active-seconds … duty cycle", and 6,240,000 requests at 10 rps is 624,000 s, not 62,000 s; (ii) 40 × 62,000 = 2,480,000, not 2,560,000 — the printed chain does not even multiply out; (iii) the correct bound is 40 × 624,000 = 24,960,000 = 24.96M requests/month, so "24,960 requests/month" and "to the right of 24,960 on the x-axis" are both wrong by 10³. The parenthetical "(6,240,000 requests × 10 rps)" also has the wrong operator: requests ÷ rate = seconds. The paragraph's own logic confirms 24.96M is intended: it asserts the 6.2–10.4M break-even band and the canonical 6.24M both lie INSIDE the feasible region, which is only true if the bound is 2.496×10^7 (a bound of 2.496×10^4 or 2.56×10^6 would put the canonical volume outside the feasible region and contradict the paragraph).
evidence: Recomputed: 6,240,000 ÷ 10 = 624,000 s (matches the page's own later "624,000-active-seconds"); 40 × 624,000 = 24,960,000 req/mo = 24.96M; 40 × 62,000 = 2,480,000 ≠ 2,560,000 (printed); 24,960,000 < 10^8 (plot range) and > 10.4M (break-even high end) — consistent with the shaded region starting at 2.496×10^7. Cross-check of the "24× shape" sentence: 40 rps × 2,592,000 s (30 days) = 103,680,000 ≈ 103.7M, which is the same construction with a full-month window, corroborating that the canonical window is 624,000 s and the bound is 24.96M.
acceptance_test: Correct the chain to "40 × 624,000 = 24,960,000 = 24.96M requests/month" and change "to the right of 24,960 on the x-axis" to "to the right of 24.96M (2.5×10^7)"; change "(6,240,000 requests × 10 rps)" to "(6,240,000 requests ÷ 10 rps = 624,000 s)". Then open the figure and verify its shaded/labeled infeasible region begins at 2.496×10^7 on the x-axis, that the 6.2M–10.4M band and the 6.24M canonical marker fall to the LEFT of that boundary, and that the 10^8 axis limit is unchanged. If the figure was drawn from the printed (wrong) bound, redraw it — this is the single most consequential figure/prose mismatch in this batch.

figure: Figure 16.1 (TCO break-even, 21-host fleet)
issue: The figure caption's parenthetical for the managed-API cost at the canonical volume is numerically inconsistent with the figure's own price and geometry. The caption states "$20.80 per 1,000 requests (~$5,816.93/mo at 6.24M req/mo)". acceptance_test: Replace the parenthetical with the derived value (~$129,792/mo, or '~$129.8K/mo') and confirm by recomputation that 6,240 x $20.80 = $129,792; confirm no other occurrence of '5,816.93' remains in Ch. 16 or its notes; confirm the caption's 'self-host sits above the API' claim still holds (155.8K > 129.8K).

figure: Figure 16.1 (right-hand shaded region, 'INFEASIBLE (> 24.96M)')

figure: Figure 16.1 (caption)
issue: The caption is overloaded and partly ungrammatical. It runs to roughly 230 words and simultaneously carries (a) the takeaway, (b) the cloud-marker caveat, (c) a 'Geometry/source' provenance clause, (d) a derivation pointer, and (e) a two-sentence availability/scope caveat that belongs in Note 16.1.1. The availability clause also contains a broken sentence: 'the canonical workload is own 99.97% multi-region active-active SLA (Ch 4) is UNTESTED and NOT PROVED here' (two copulas, missing possessive). A reader who reads only the caption gets a dense, partly unparsable block; a reader who reads only the figure gets none of the caveats.
evidence: Rendered page inspection of the caption block under Figure 16.1; the sentence 'every line is a single-region cost - the canonical workload is own 99.97% multi-region active-active SLA (Ch 4) is UNTESTED and NOT PROVED here; failover is N-1 single-host only with no region-failure test, and the three modes are not compared on matched availability/SLO/warm-capacity assumptions (Table 16-1, Sec 16.3).'
acceptance_test: Reduce the caption to at most three sentences (takeaway + one scope qualifier + pointer to Note 16.1.1), move the availability/scope caveat into Note 16.1.1, and repair the broken clause to 'the canonical workload's own 99.97% multi-region active-active SLA (Ch 4) is UNTESTED and NOT PROVED here'. Confirm the caption still contains the 'not apples-to-apples' warning and the pointer to the note.

figure: Figure 16.1 (legend text and in-plot annotation boxes)
issue: The legend text and the four in-plot annotation boxes appear to be set below the 8 pt print floor for figure in-text annotations. At the 150 dpi rendering the legend glyphs are roughly half the height of the body text on the same page, which corresponds to approximately 6-7 pt at US Letter. The legend carries the figure's key numeric results ($155.8K/mo, $87.6K/mo, $20.80/1K, 7.5M, 6.2-10.4M) and the annotation boxes carry the caveats, so legibility is load-bearing here, not decorative.
evidence: Rendered page inspection at 150 dpi: legend text height is visibly ~55-60% of the 10.5 pt body text height on the same page; the same ratio holds for the 'break-even = 7.5M', 'sensitivity = 6.2-10.4M', 'canonical 6.24M req/mo' and 'cloud $87.6K/mo' boxes. This is an estimate from the rendering, not a measurement of the source font size.
acceptance_test: Measure the source font size of the legend and annotation text; if any is below 8 pt at final trim size, raise it to >= 8 pt (or move the annotation text into the caption/note and keep only short in-figure labels). Re-render at 150 dpi and confirm the legend is readable at 100% print size without magnification.

figure: Figure 16.1 (legend swatches and in-plot hatching)
issue: Grayscale distinguishability is weak in two places. (a) The managed-API centerline ($20.80/1K) is a red dashed line drawn inside the red hatched price band; in grayscale both collapse to similar mid-gray and the centerline is difficult to separate from the band texture. (b) The infeasible region uses a gray hatch that is visually similar in weight to the price band's hatch, so in grayscale the two hatched regions may read as the same texture. The legend also uses red for three different entries (price band, managed line, break-even, sensitivity), so color alone is currently carrying distinctions that texture should carry.
evidence: Rendered page inspection; the figure's own caption states 'Geometry/source: log-cost/month vs requests/month' and the legend distinguishes series primarily by hue (red/blue/green).
acceptance_test: Convert the figure to grayscale and confirm that (i) the managed centerline is distinguishable from the price band, (ii) the infeasible region is distinguishable from the price band, and (iii) every legend entry maps to a uniquely identifiable plotted element. If not, differentiate by texture/dash pattern/line weight rather than hue.

figure: Figure 16.1 (x-axis range)
issue: The x-axis spans 1e4 to 1e8 requests/month, but the entire decision-relevant region (canonical 6.24M, sensitivity 6.2-10.4M, break-even 7.5M, feasible max 24.96M) occupies roughly the rightmost 20% of the axis, while the two leftmost decades are empty of any annotation or comparison. The reader must scan a mostly empty plot to find the crossing, and the 6.2M-10.4M sensitivity interval (a factor of 1.7) is compressed into a sliver.
evidence: Rendered page inspection: the blue/red crossing and the green diamond sit between the 1e6 and 1e7 gridlines, with the 1e4-1e6 region containing no marked feature.
acceptance_test: Tighten the x-limits (e.g. 3e6 to 1e8) or add an inset/zoom panel over 5M-30M, and confirm that the canonical point, the sensitivity band, the break-even marker and the feasible-max line are all visually separated and legible.

figure: Figure 16.1 (annotation boxes)
issue: The four annotation boxes are clustered in the upper-left of the plot, far from the features they describe, and none has a leader line. 'break-even = 7.5M' sits roughly three decades to the left of the actual crossing it names; 'canonical 6.24M req/mo' and 'cloud $87.6K/mo (occupancy input) priced at 6.24M req/mo only' sit above and left of the green diamond. The reader must map text to features by value-matching rather than by spatial proximity, which is the slowest and least reliable reading mode for a diagram.
evidence: Rendered page inspection: the annotation block occupies the region x ~ 1e4-1e6, y ~ 1e5-1e6, while the crossing is at x ~ 7.5M and the diamond at x = 6.24M, y = 8.76e4.
acceptance_test: Reposition each annotation adjacent to its feature (or add leader lines), and confirm that each annotation can be associated with its target without reading the numeric values.

figure: Figure 16.1 ('feasible max 24.96M' label)
issue: The 'feasible max 24.96M' label states a result without its derivation, and the derivation (40 rps x 624,000 active s/mo) appears nowhere on the figure. The reader cannot check the bound from the figure, and the number's relation to the x-axis label ('duration varied at FIXED 40 rps peak') is exactly the ambiguity flagged in FIG-16.1-02. The 'canonical 6.24M req/mo' annotation likewise omits the corresponding 10 rps average rate.
evidence: Rendered page inspection: the top-of-plot label reads 'feasible max 24.96M' with no supporting expression; the derivation is only in Note 16.1.1 on PDF p. 294.
acceptance_test: Add the derivation to the label or the annotation, e.g. 'feasible max 24.96M req/mo (40 rps x 624,000 active s/mo)', and 'canonical 6.24M req/mo (10 rps avg)'. Confirm the arithmetic 40 x 624,000 = 24,960,000 and 6,240,000/624,000 = 10 rps.

figure: Figure 16.1 (legend entry 1)
issue: The legend entry 'price band $15-25/1K' does not say whose price band it is. In a figure that also contains a self-host cost line, a cloud cost marker, and a managed-API line, an unqualified 'price band' is ambiguous: it is the managed-API price band (the sensitivity range 6.2M-10.4M derives from it), not a band of self-host cost. The reader could plausibly read it as a band of self-host TCO.
evidence: Rendered page inspection of the legend; the caption and Note 16.1.1 both attribute the $15-25/1K range to the managed API price sensitivity ('Sensitivity: a $15-25/1K price band moves the break-even to ~6.2-10.4M req/mo').
acceptance_test: Rename the legend entry to 'managed API price band $15-25/1K' and confirm no other series in the figure is described as a price band.

figure: Note 16.1.1 (the note that defines Figure 16.1's series and bounds)
issue: Note 16.1.1 contains two garbled constructions that directly define Figure 16.1 and would mislead a reader auditing the figure. (a) 'The feasible served-volume bound (40 rps x 624,000 canonical active s x 24.96M req/mo)' uses a multiplication sign where an equality is meant; read literally it asserts that the bound is the product of 40 rps, 624,000 s and 24.96M requests, which is off by a factor of 24.96M. (b) 'the case (0) /KV-screen line = the case (i) 12-host line, $162,760.59/mo, is priced in Sec 16.3 but not plotted' asserts an identity between case (0) (the plotted $155.8K/mo 21-host line) and case (i) (a 12-host line at $162,760.59/mo that is explicitly not plotted); the two cannot both be true, and the sentence's scope is ambiguous as to which line is flat and which is unplotted. A third fragment, 'for the 21-host peak KV-screen fleet = zero spare', leaves '= zero spare' dangling.
evidence: Rendered page inspection of Note 16.1.1 on PDF p. 294; the figure's own legend and caption identify the plotted self-host series as '$155.8K/mo (21 hosts)' and the caption calls it 'case 0', while the note assigns $162,760.59/mo to case (i) and says it is not plotted.
acceptance_test: Rewrite (a) as '40 rps x 624,000 canonical active s = 24.96M req/mo' and (b) as 'the case (0) /KV-screen line (plotted, $155.8K/mo) - the case (i) 12-host line, $162,760.59/mo, is priced in Sec 16.3 but not plotted - is flat because the fleet is paid regardless of volume'. Confirm that exactly one self-host series is plotted and that its value ($155.8K/mo) matches the legend and caption.

figure: Figure 16.1 (caption) vs Note 16.1.1 (PDF p. 294)
issue: Case labels drift between the caption and the note: the caption writes 'case 0' (arabic, no parentheses) while the note writes 'case (0)' and 'case (i)' (roman numeral in parentheses). The reader cannot tell whether 'case 0' and 'case (i)' are the same enumeration scheme, and the caption's parenthetical '($155.8K/mo, case 0) /KV-screen sensitivity line' uses a slash as an undeclared separator in a way that reads as a typo.
evidence: Rendered page inspection: caption on PDF p. 298 reads 'case 0'; Note 16.1.1 on PDF p. 294 reads 'case (0)' and 'case (i)'. The slash separator appears in both places ('case (0) /KV-screen line').
acceptance_test: Adopt one enumeration convention (e.g. 'case 0', 'case 1') and use it in the caption, the note, Table 16-1 and Sec 16.3; replace the slash separator with a dash or parentheses. Confirm no remaining 'case (i)' / 'case (0)' forms.
